title: 3 animals that see the world differently

scenes.headline: 3 animals that see the world differently.
Each eye moves on its own.
scenes.body: Nearly 360° view. Coiled optic nerves give its eyes slack to swivel.
scenes.source: Florida Museum; Collins et al. 2025, Sci. Rep.

scenes.headline: Turns its head up to 270° each way.
scenes.body: 14 neck vertebrae (you have 7) and blood reservoirs keep its brain supplied.

scenes.headline: No blind spot.
scenes.body: Its retina is wired the other way round: nerves run behind the light-sensing cells, not in front.

scenes.headline: You have a blind spot in each eye.
scenes.body: It's where your optic nerve passes through the retina.

caption:
Three animals whose eyes break the rules.

The owl findings come from Johns Hopkins scans of snowy, barred and great horned owls; 12 of their 14 neck vertebrae have extra room around the main artery.

Sources: Florida Museum of Natural History; Johns Hopkins (Science, 2013); UC Berkeley Understanding Evolution. Footage: great horned owl. Photos/video: Wikimedia Commons (credits on screen).
notes: Numbered list where every item adds a mechanism, and the last line turns the lens on the viewer's own eye.
